references.text: The Israelites cried out to God during their slavery in Egypt, and God heard their cry of distress and saw their suffering—the original event referred to in Deuteronomy 26:7.
The Lord tells Moses that He has seen the misery of His people, heard their cry, and knows their sufferings—using the same language about seeing, hearing, and knowing the people's distress.
God remembers His covenant and has heard the Israelites' complaints about slavery—confirming that God heard the people's cry.
The Israelites recall how they cried out to the Lord, He heard their voice, and brought them out of Egypt—the same historical confession.
Nehemiah reminds us that God saw the ancestors' misery in Egypt and heard their cry at the Red Sea.
The suffering one cries out to the Lord, and the Lord does not hide His face but hears when he calls—a thematic parallel about God hearing the cries of those in distress.
The afflicted cried out, and the Lord heard and saved him from all his trouble—the same theme of God hearing and answering cries for help.
God looked upon them in their affliction and heard their cry of distress—summarizing God's faithful response to Israel's cries throughout history.
Stephen quotes God's words that He has seen the oppression of His people in Egypt and heard their groaning—a direct reference to the same event.
